lead: Augmented reality (AR) adds computer-made objects to a live view of the real world and keeps each object fixed to a real place. It exists because information is easier to use when it sits on the thing it describes: a machine on a factory floor, a page in a book, a street ahead. This chapter gives the three tests that separate AR from a simple video overlay, the features and classic methods, and the block architecture every AR system follows.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 on what VR, AR, MR and XR are, and the three I's.

sections.h3: The three tests that define AR

blocks.text: Augmented reality (AR) is a live view of the real world with computer-made objects added to it, where each virtual object stays tied to a real place. Virtual reality (VR) replaces the real view with a synthetic one. Mixed reality (MR) is the wider blend of real and virtual; AR is one region of MR.

The reality–virtuality continuum runs from the real environment, through AR, through augmented virtuality (mostly virtual, with real video or objects added), to the virtual environment. AR sits near the real end: the real world is still the main view.
Three tests separate AR from an overlay:

items: It combines real and virtual light in one view.
It registers virtual objects in 3D, so they stay fixed to real points as the user moves.
It runs in real time, updating the overlay as the user moves.

blocks.text: A phone camera that pastes a sticker at a fixed screen position fails test 2. A face filter that follows the nose passes. Registration needs a pose: the position and orientation of the camera or head in the world. Pose has six degrees of freedom (6DoF): x, y, z for position and yaw, pitch, roll for orientation.
Some syllabi call this set of tests the 'taxonomy of AR' or 'AR systems and functionality'.

sections.h3: Features and the classic AR methods

blocks.text: Features follow from the tests. 3D registration locks virtual objects to world coordinates, not screen coordinates. Real-time response means the pose is estimated and the frame redrawn every 16–33 ms for 30–60 frames per second. Context awareness uses what the system sees or where it is — a printed marker, a detected plane, a GPS point — to choose content. Hands-free use matters when the user is holding a tool or a patient.
The classic AR methods are four:

items: Optical see-through: a half-silvered combiner in front of the eye lets real light pass and reflects a micro-display into the eye. The user sees the real world directly, with virtual light added.
Video see-through: a camera captures the real scene, the renderer adds virtual objects to that image, and a screen shows the mix. Phone AR and most headsets with closed displays use this.
Monitor-based: a fixed camera looks at the scene and a desktop monitor shows the mixed view, like a window into the world.
Projection-based (spatial AR): a projector throws light onto the real surface, so the surface itself carries the virtual content. No display is worn.

blocks.text: Visualization techniques are the drawing choices: text labels pinned to objects, arrows for direction, ghosted or X-ray models, and full 3D models. Wireless displays help education: a tablet shows the overlay while the camera stands on a desk, so students pass it around. See 6.2 for the optics and 6.3 for marker-less tracking.

sections.h3: System architecture: from light to pose to pixels

blocks.text: Every AR system follows the same loop, in this order.

items: The real world produces light and motion.
Cameras and an IMU (inertial measurement unit: accelerometer and gyroscope) measure the scene and the head.
The tracker estimates the pose.
Registration maps world points into camera coordinates.
The renderer sets its virtual camera to the same pose and draws the virtual scene.
The combiner or display shows real and virtual light together.
The user sees the overlay, moves, and the loop repeats.

blocks.where: X_world is a 3D point in world coordinates; R is a 3×3 rotation matrix; t is a 3-vector translation; X_cam is the same point in camera coordinates.

blocks.text: Inside the AR application, the scene is stored as a scene graph: a tree of transforms. The root is the world. One child is the tracked camera. Other children are virtual objects. Each node's transform places it in its parent. When the tracker updates the camera node, every virtual object keeps its world position and the view moves correctly.

items: Latency: delay between motion and updated frame. Prediction hides some of it.
Registration error: jitter and drift move the overlay off its real anchor.
Limited field of view: optical combiners often cover a narrow angle.
Changing light: a virtual object must be shaded to match the room.
Occlusion: a real hand in front of a virtual object should hide it; virtual objects should also hide real ones.
Battery and heat: cameras, tracking and rendering drain a phone.
Privacy: an always-on camera in a home or clinic sees more than the app needs.

examples.question: A head tracker updates the head angle every 50 ms. The user turns the head at 120° per second. (a) Find the angle turned during one update and the apparent slip of the overlay at a viewing distance of 2 m. (b) Find the tracker delay that keeps the slip at or below 5 mm at 2 m.
steps: Angle turned in T: Δθ = 120°/s × 0.050 s = 6.0°.
Slip at distance d = 2 m: s = d tan Δθ = 2 m × tan 6° = 2 × 0.10510 = 0.2102 m.
examples.answer: The slip is 6.0° or 21.0 cm at 2 m with a 50 ms delay; keeping it under 5 mm needs a delay of about 1.19 ms, which is shorter than a normal tracker, so the pose must be predicted.
examples.check:
import math
turn_rate = 120.0
delay = 0.050
slip_deg = turn_rate * delay
dist = 2.0
shift = dist * math.tan(math.radians(slip_deg))
allowed_shift = 0.005
theta_deg = math.degrees(math.atan(allowed_shift / dist))
allowed_delay = theta_deg / turn_rate
print(f"{slip_deg:.1f}")
print(f"{shift:.4f}")
print(f"{theta_deg:.4f}")
print(f"{allowed_delay:.6f}")

traps: Saying AR is a camera picture with a sticker pasted on top. The sticker must be registered in 3D and updated in real time.
Treating AR and VR as opposites. AR is part of the reality–virtuality continuum, and MR includes both AR and augmented virtuality.
Claiming video see-through is not real AR. A camera between eye and world still gives a combined, registered, real-time view.
Believing a higher frame rate always fixes registration. Frame rate cuts latency but cannot fix a wrong pose; drift and jitter remain.
Mixing latency and registration error. Latency is a time delay; registration error is a spatial misalignment.

quiz.q: State the three requirements of AR.
quiz.a: It combines real and virtual in one view; it registers virtual objects in 3D with the real world; it runs in real time.

quiz.q: Where does AR sit on the reality–virtuality continuum?
quiz.a: Near the real end. The real world is the main view and virtual objects are added. Augmented virtuality is the opposite: mostly virtual with real elements added.

quiz.q: A tracker updates every 30 ms. The head turns at 90° per second. Find the angle turned in one update and the slip at 1.5 m.
Why does the worked example force the system to predict the pose rather than just use a faster display?
quiz.a: The allowed delay is about 1.19 ms, shorter than normal tracker and display pipelines. A faster display alone cannot reach it, so the system estimates the future head pose and renders for that predicted pose.

quiz.q: Give one difference and one cost between optical and video see-through.
quiz.a: Optical see-through lets real light reach the eye directly, so the real view is bright and has no camera latency; the combiner dims the real view and limits field of view. Video see-through can match brightness and hide real objects, but the camera adds latency and limits resolution.

quiz.q: Why is occlusion hard in video see-through AR?
quiz.a: To let a real object hide a virtual one, the system needs the depth of the real scene. Without depth, the renderer draws the virtual object over the real image even when the real object is in front.

quiz.q: Name the four classic AR methods.
quiz.a: Optical see-through, video see-through, monitor-based, and projection-based (spatial AR).

quiz.q: An app draws a label at a fixed screen corner over a live camera feed. Which AR test fails, and why?
quiz.a: 3D registration fails. The label is fixed to the screen, not to a world point, so it does not stay on the real object when the camera moves.

beyond: Not for the exam. Current work moves registration from one device to a shared map: AR Cloud and visual positioning systems let many phones agree on the same world coordinates. Depth sensors and scene understanding add real occlusion. WebXR makes AR run in a browser. Privacy rules now treat camera pose data as personal data. Search for 'visual positioning system', 'WebXR hit test' and 'AR occlusion depth API'.
